question: A 3-year-old girl has growth failure, pale bulky floating stools, and iron-deficiency anaemia since weaning onto wheat-based foods at 9 months. Anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA (anti-tTG IgA) comes back negative. Which ONE statement BEST guides the next step?

answers.text: A negative anti-tTG IgA definitively excludes coeliac disease; investigate for other causes of malabsorption.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. A negative anti-tTG IgA does NOT definitively exclude coeliac disease if IgA deficiency has not been ruled out. IgA deficiency is the most commonly missed confounder in coeliac serology.

answers.text: Check total serum IgA level — if IgA-deficient, the anti-tTG IgA will be falsely negative and IgG-based tests (anti-DGP IgG or anti-tTG IgG) should be used instead.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Selective IgA deficiency occurs in 1:400 individuals (10× more common in coeliac disease patients). If total IgA is low (<0.07 g/L), anti-tTG IgA will be falsely negative. In this setting, use anti-deamidated gliadin peptide IgG (anti-DGP IgG) or anti-tTG IgG. Duodenal biopsy (showing villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, increased intraepithelial lymphocytes) remains the gold standard for diagnosis.

answers.text: Repeat the anti-tTG IgA after 6 months on a gluten-free diet — it will turn positive once gluten is reintroduced.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. A gluten-free diet should NOT be started before the diagnostic work-up is complete. Removing gluten causes antibody levels to fall and villous atrophy to heal, making subsequent testing unreliable. Always complete serology and biopsy ON a gluten-containing diet.

answers.text: Proceed directly to small bowel biopsy because serology is unreliable in young children under 5 years.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Serology (anti-tTG IgA + total IgA) is the validated first-line test and IS reliable in children over 2 years. Biopsy is the gold standard and is indicated after positive serology (or when serology is falsely negative due to IgA deficiency). Bypassing serology entirely is not the current standard of care.

overallFeedback.feedback: Key trap: anti-tTG IgA is falsely negative in IgA deficiency. ALWAYS measure total serum IgA alongside anti-tTG IgA. If IgA-deficient, use IgG-based tests. Never start a gluten-free diet before completing the diagnostic workup — it invalidates serology and biopsy results.

Correct. The most commonly missed step in coeliac screening is forgetting to measure total serum IgA alongside anti-tTG IgA. IgA deficiency causes a false-negative anti-tTG IgA. Always pair them. Diagnosis is confirmed by duodenal biopsy (modified Marsh criteria); treatment is lifelong gluten-free diet.
